projects.title: OneSearch | 3rd Place @ HackMIT
projects.description: • Won 3rd Place in Y Combinator Track (from 250+); 1 of 2 teams invited to YC Office Hours to develop prototype• Reduced file retrieval time by 99% (30+ min to <3 sec) by deploying a Next.js app on Vercel with semantic search across Google Drive, Dropbox, and local storage• Led 25+ user research interviews, translated insights to product features and responsive UI/UX

projects.title: Agora | PennApps
projects.description: • Built an AI-powered conversational assistant that unifies fragmented campus and organizational data into instant, trusted natural-language answers, eliminating the need to search across dozens of sites and PDFs• Designed and implemented a scalable RAG architecture (Django + FastAPI + vector database) with automated web scraping, semantic search, and source attribution for transparent, verifiable responses • Developed systems for data freshness and reliability, including scheduled re-indexing, expiration tracking, and continuous monitoring to ensure up-to-date information at scale

projects.title: Illuminating STEM | Lead Artist and Interviewer
projects.description: • Created 4 paintings inspired by the Picture Superiority effect to make science more accessible through art• Secured interviews with 4 noted scientists from CDC, MIT, UW, and NOAA in diverse fields, from biogeochemistry to infectious disease transmission• Designed artwork that represented the scientists' work and unique journeys in STEM, highlighting their contributions• Artwork displayed at the Sammamish City Library as part of the “Visualizing STEM: An Artistic Perspective” exhibition

projects.title: RePurpose | 1st Place @ Washington State Science & Engineering Fair
projects.description: • Reduced early-stage cancer R&D timelines by 30%; discovered 145 FDA-approved drug candidates for repurposing• Achieved 99% accuracy; trained a TensorFlow/Keras sequential neural network on 146K+ chemical compounds• Outperformed baseline models by 10–15% in classifying anticancer vs. no anticancer activity; designed experimental process optimization via Bayesian hyperparameter search across 20+ architectures

projects.title: Reimagining Blood Drawing | 3rd Place @ Washington State Science & Engineering Fair
projects.description: • Designed an innovative hypodermic needle inspired by mosquito proboscises to minimize patient discomfort. • Incorporated dissolvable microneedles and vibration technology for a cost-effective and user-friendly solution. • Conducted an economic analysis showing the design’s affordability after 30 uses compared to traditional needles.

Brb, I’m dropping $1,199 to use an app 😭 I was sitting with Anika Halappanavar in Carnegie Mellon University - Tepper School of Business when she told me there was an event in the Swartz Center in just 15 minutes. So what was I actually *supposed* to do for the next few hours? Lock myself in my dorm to study for my cooked Data Structures and Algorithms final. I’m so, so glad I didn’t. I’m so glad that my curiosity got the better of me, and that I turned around and walked up those stairs. Because that’s the day I learned about Sonder . And the amazing team behind them— Harvin Park , Foy Dosunmu , and Eunice Lai —that’s spending every day to build a new way, for everyone, to tell their stories. They’re literally building to bring memories to life. For as long as I’ve used Sonder, it’s only been available on an Apple Mac. Spoiler: I don’t have one. But my younger brother does, and it means I’ve fought with him way too many times to use his computer, just so I could update my memory graph or ask the Narrator another question. Cue me genuinely debating buying a MacBook for $1,199, with my Boeing internship money 😭 But I don’t have to anymore :) Sonder launched on the App Store earlier this week, and if you’re going to Y Combinator Startup School with me, they’re throwing! To the Sonder team, huge congrats on the launch 🥹 (and a personal thank you from my bank account, lol) Can’t wait to fill my Startup School arc with all the memories from this trip 🫶 ...more

A picture is worth a thousand words? More like, a solid portfolio is worth a thousand resumes (you get the point 🤪) This is how I’m building my portfolio before recruiting is in full swing, and how you can build yours too :) Yesterday, I told you about requirements: that helped me nail the content for my portfolio. I want to talk about the design part today, 𝘀𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗙𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝟱 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲-𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝟭𝟵𝘁𝗵. I saw a video where Nick Saraev generated 25 website designs with Fable and was genuinely blown away (!) So I tried it out with building my portfolio and generated 25 design directions in one afternoon. I put two constraints on Fable first: 𝗦𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁. This is the mistake I actually made the first time: I gave Fable everything I had written about my projects and asked it for 25 directions. But because I was trying to solve two problems at once, I was basically getting mush (and blowing through *way* more tokens than I’d like to admit). When I ran it again, this time with just design + only the titles of my projects, it finally worked :) 𝗗𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗼𝘂𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝗼, 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝘆𝗹𝗲. I learned that I like seeing all my projects in one glance. But you might like a carousel structure, which goes through your projects one by one. We’re not going to know until we’ve seen both. 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗧𝗟𝗗𝗥: I think you’ve got pretty good taste. You’ll see something and know immediately if you like it or not. But it’s way harder to imagine your way to what you like, and you definitely can’t give feedback on something that doesn’t exist yet. These were some of the directions I got—guess which one I went with :) I'll reveal it tomorrow, along with how I'm building out the components. Full prompt I used for this + Nick’s video is in the comments! ...more

I’m so cooked if my mom sees this. At midnight, when she told me to go to bed, I said “yes.” In all fairness, I also thought I was going to sleep. I pulled an all-nighter instead, and she has no idea. Yet. To do what? Fill up two pages of grid paper. That’s the photo. Yesterday, I told you that code should be the last thing you write. 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗴𝗼: 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲. This is the first stage of my portfolio. 𝗜 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝘆 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰-𝗱𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 (𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗯𝗶𝗻𝗲𝗱) and none of it is writing code. That still surprises people (and me too, honestly). But it’s made me realize that requirements are the building. The code is just what *happens* to fall out at the end. 𝗜 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗯𝘆 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝗺𝗽𝗶𝗻𝗴 (𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴) 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 + 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺 𝗜’𝗺 𝘁𝗿𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲. I’ve found Wispr Flow super helpful for this (not an ad lol). I just talk out loud and brain dump as I speak. 𝗗𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝗮𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗯𝗹𝗲. It’s always better to get everything out, then go back to refine, because I guarantee you’ll miss out on 1) important ideas 2) connections if you don’t give yourself space to word vomit first. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗜 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻. I have the agent start asking me questions about my brain dump. We go back and forth, with follow-up questions from both of us. Emphasis on questions, not answers. 𝗔 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘁𝗼 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝘆𝗲𝘁 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺. That’s the whole point of this stage: not writing down what you’ve already decided, but finding what you haven’t. I’m writing the whole time: the requirements as they become clearer + new questions as I have as I learn more. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿. The method is what matters: ramble, get interviewed, and capture the requirements as they form (wherever you do this). If you’re solving a problem, believe in your ability to articulate it and go deep into what it’s actually about. That becomes unbelievably clear here. 𝗜𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆: open whatever coding tool you already use and start a new project. Instead of telling it what to build, do the brain dump exercise first: ramble out loud about something you’ve been thinking about starting, then let it ask you questions. You don’t have to finish every single stage today: the goal is to just get you to see what the start of a requirements file looks like, and what it means for a problem you care about. Comment “QUESTIONS” or send me a DM so I can send you the prompt I use for generating specific questions! ...more

I’m at Boeing this summer, and untested code here isn’t an option. A mistake here can mean real changes to certification. Those are very real changes to safety for very real people: my friends and family who fly on Boeing planes every day. 𝗦𝗼 𝗜 𝗵𝗮𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝗻𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗜’𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀 (𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝟭𝟬+ 𝗵𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗻𝘀!). I think you’ll recognize it :) I’d open Cursor , send an extensive first prompt, and then spend the next hours screenshotting + going back and forth, until I had something that demoed great. It definitely looked finished, but I wanted to build things that would actually outlast 48 hours. The change I made was 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰-𝗱𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗽𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗮 𝗳𝗶𝘃𝗲-𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 I learned with Kiro (agentic IDE built by Amazon ). Instead of spending minutes in plan-mode, I got a grid-paper notebook and spent a day thinking on paper before I started writing any code. It doesn’t have to take you that long or even be on paper. But the practice pushes you to front-load your planning, so the execution becomes the easy part. 𝗧𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆’𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄, 𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗴𝗲: 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀. 𝗜𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼𝗱𝗮𝘆: next time you open the coding IDE you use ( Claude Code , Cursor, etc.), pause before you type! See if you want to tell it immediately what to build. Naming what you actually want first, in a structured process (like spec-driven development) is actually what saves you the hours of back-and-forth later. 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗜 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱: Two YouTube videos (see the comment!). And if you’re a college student (me me me), check if Kiro partners with your school to get it free for a whole year! I’m always happy to share more detail. If you want to know more, don’t be shy! Send me a DM or write a comment :) ...more

I just wish you weren’t reading this post. I wish you were reading the one I’ll eventually write about: • 𝗛𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗠𝗜𝗧. The 48 hours where the startup world became unmistakably real to me. Third place in the YC track. And a five-minute conversation at the Eigen Labs booth that became my first PM internship, which became two agents Dokimos and Nostos, which became second place and $1,000 on a demo day stage. • Going through 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗽 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝘂𝗯𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀, 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗼 𝗱𝗮𝘆, and this summer with the most phenomenal and kindest engineers I know, Cady ( Shuyao He ) and Raveena Gupta . • 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗛𝗮𝗰𝗸𝘀. Where I got to build for the ADHD community and brought a new definition of “calendar” to life. • 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝘆 𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲𝗲𝗿, and in essence, my life: Adam Paulisick , Dave Mawhinney , Charles Johnson, Aaron Tainter . • Certifying hundreds of Boeing aircrafts. Painstakingly making the architecture decisions for part of this system, and then being the very person who starts implementing them. • Writing the 1,689 words I’ll remember for the rest of my life. These are incredible stories I can’t wait to share. But I realized that if I waited until I’d written each one perfectly, then agonized over editing it, then made it sound “right,” then calculated the absolute perfect cadence to push them out, post by post…I’d miss the chance to share the journey I’m actually on right now, in real time. I’m spending this summer building agentic systems. Not just because my internship has given me the opportunity to, as part of an amazing systems engineering team at Boeing—but because I’ve used Cursor, Windsurf (and more!) across 10+ hackathons, and implementation just isn’t the bottleneck anymore. We’ve raised $500K from a16z speedrun ! It’s crazy I finally get to share this. I’ve wanted to write that sentence since I was 10. I used to binge-watch Shark Tank, keep a list with hundreds of startup ideas, and doodle future logos in my school notebooks. Then I moved to the US to study at UIUC, and things started feeling real. I met Ansh , we boiled ramen in his kettle together, and started building things that fascinated us. (Completely ruined the kettle btw.) Somewhere between campus pitches, hackathons, and a lot of questionable product ideas, I got incredibly lucky with mentors who kept taking my ideas seriously long before they deserved to be. Andrew D'Souza and the Boardy team took a bet on me. They gave me my first real glimpse of what it looks like when people are completely obsessed with something they’re building. I wanted that for myself. Ansh and I built our first prototype for ChatOverflow in February. Four weeks later, we were backed by a16z speedrun. A huge thank you to my friends who tolerated my worst startup ideas at 2am before a final; to my teachers who believed in me really early on; and to my family, who have always supported me, forever smiling (sometimes nervously), even through the occasional “maybe I should drop out” conversations : ) Now loving every moment of speedrun with Fareed Mosavat , Andrew Chen , Jonathan Lai , Troy Kirwin , Joan DeGennaro , Samira Behrouzan , Tabish Gilani , Macy Mills , Jordan Mazer , Jordan Carver , Lester Chen , Tom Hammer , and so many more. You guys make speedrun ridiculously fun. Back to building! 🚀

The best investment you can make is in someone else's future. The past few weeks have reminded me that some of the most meaningful work you can do is helping others take the first step toward their goals. At Pillars Network , I spoke about finding a problem that's actually worth solving, and solving it for the right reasons. At ISNA Canada 's YouthX, I shared what it takes to go from recognizing a problem to creating a solution. At the DMV Hackathon organized by Riwayah.Ai , I had the opportunity to mentor and judge students as they brought their ideas to life. And tomorrow at Buildojo , I'll be helping the next generation identify meaningful problems and take the first steps toward solving them. Every one of these experiences has reinforced the same lesson. There isn't a shortage of talented young people. What's often missing is someone who believes in them early, asks the right questions, and gives them the confidence to begin. One conversation can change the direction of someone's future. That's the best investment you can make.

I almost didn’t go to YC Startup School this year. I’ve already been once. What else could I learn this time? Turns out, a LOT. 4 days in SF gave me more value than the previous 4 months. I met incredible builders and got recognized by Alexandr Wang and Garry Tan . I spent late nights with founders at Corgi Cafe turning shower thoughts into prototypes. Every conversation sparked more ideas and more energy. I forgot how magical it feels to be surrounded by people who are this obsessed about building. Sure, you can find all the talks on YouTube. But it was never about the talks. You had to be there to experience the magic. I’m grateful to YC for bringing so many founders into one place. You can’t find this level of talent density anywhere else in the world. On my return flight, I felt whiplash and reflected deeply on everything. I spent 3 more days cleaning up my notes and decided to turn them into something I hope others could find helpful. The article is finally out. I hope it will inspire at least one person to start building. Thanks, YC. -🪀

i don't want to be impressive for my age. i want to be impressive. there's this quote i love: "at some point, we ask of the piano-playing dog, not 'are you a dog?' but 'are you any good at playing the piano?'" usually when i meet someone, we talk about what i'm working on. oro, content, building, whatever. the conversation flows normally. then at some point i mention my age, and suddenly the energy shifts. "wait, you're doing really good for a first-year!" i get why they say it. it sounds like a compliment. but here's what i hear: we didn't expect much from you. i don't want my age to be a crutch. something that excuses the gaps or inflates the wins. i want to be judged on what i actually built, not on what's surprising given my birth year. if i'm doing something well, i want it to be because i'm doing it well. if i'm not, i want to know that too. the age qualifier blurs the lines for both. i'd rather you forget how old i am entirely. just tell me if i'm any good at the piano.
